Baker, on Vice Admiral of the Blue, Henry Hill. This gallant officer, who entered the navy in 1787, was midshipman of the Phoenix in her action with the French ship Resole, in the Hast Indies, in 1701 ; and subsequently distinguished himself in the West Indies. He was lieutenant of the Zebra at the reduction of the French islands there, and was warmly engaged on shore in their caplure. He served with the storming parties on a great many occasions, and particularly itt storming Fort Royal, Martinique, in 1704 In the loiiowtng year lie was engaged in quelling an insurrection at St. Vincent's. In that affair lie was severely wounded, and had a pension of 250/, per annum granted to iiun for wounds in 1815.

Death in a Grave. þÿ On Saturday morning last an awful event occurred in the burialground belonging to the Society of Friends in Baker's row, Whtlechapel. It appears that about 12 o'clock Mr Gf orge Stevens, the sexton, about 50 years of ngn, had descended a newly dug grave lor the purpose ol seeing that the bottom was perfectly level, a precaution in which the Friends are very particular. In about an hour after his maid servant went to call him into the house, hut not seeing him about the ground, she went and looked down the newly dug grave, when she was horror struck at discovering her m is'' r lying at the bottom, insensible. An alarm was given, and the body was got up, and two medical gentlemen were called in, but all hopes of restoring Itiin were past, as he had been dead some time.

Seen from the deck ol the vessel, th0 jsland had the appearance of a mass of rocks, but a neater approach showed it to be an island, covered with cocoa nut trees, with thick underbush. When convinced that was an island, Captain Simmons supposed it might be one already known, and at first mistook it for Carisloot. He lowered his boat and attempted to land, but was prevented by a reef of black coral rocks, with heavy breakers, which surrounded the island. Ho went completely round it, however, and found it to be about six miles in circumference. At a short distance from it he found no sounding in 60 fathoms of water. þÿ After examining it for two or three hoorsf he steered tor Carisfoot, according to his reckoning, made it in the course of a few hours, and passed to the south of it. A large lagoon was in the middle of the island, which seemed to be rich and fertile. On reaching Valparaiso, he waited upon the commander of the British squadron and informed linn of the discovery. It is situate in the track from Otaheite to Valparaiso, in south latitude 21 degrees and 10 minutes, and west longitude 1 3N degrees.")! minutes He named it the Isle of Faith, from his vessel."

A Coffe Plantation in Cuba. þÿ A coffee estate is indeed a peilect garden, surpassing iri beauty aught that the bleak climate of England can produce. Imagine more than three hundred acres of land planted in regular squares, with evenly pruned shrubs, each containing about eight acres, intersected by broad alleys of palms, oranges, mangoes, and other beautiful irees, the interslices between which are planted with lenmns pomegranates, Cape jessamines, tube roses, lilies, and vatious Other gaudy and fragrant flowers; while a double strip of guinea grass, or of luscious lines, skill the sides, presenting a putty contrast to the smooth red soil in ihe centre, sc upulously kept free Irom ail venture Then the beauty of the whole while in the flower þÿ that of the coffee, white, and so abundant, that the fitbls seem covered with flukes of

snow : the fringe like blossoms of the roe apples; the red ol the pomegranate and Mexican rose; the laige scarlet flowers of the pinion, which, when m bloom, coveting the whole tree wuh a flaming coat, is the richest of þÿMora srealm ; the quaint litio's trumpet sharped flowers, painted yellow and red, bursting in bunches from the blunt extremities of each leafless branch; the young pine apples, wiih blue flowerets projecting from the cenue ot ilieir squares; the white tube roses, and double Cape jessamines, the gaudy vellovv flag, and a score of other flowers known to us only by the sickly tenants of the hot house. And when some ot the flowers have given place to the ripened fruit, and the golden oiange, the yellow mangoe, the lime, the lemon, the luscious caimiio, and sugared zapote: the mellow avocado pear, the custard apple, and the rose apple, giving to the palate the flavour of otto of roses ; when all these hang on the trees in oppressive abundance, and the ground is also covered with the over ripe, the owner of a coffee estate might safely challenge the world for a fairer garden. Nor must this be thought the appearance it presents for only a short period. The coflee has successive crops of blossoms live or six times in the waiter and spring, and of the orange, the ripe fruit and blossoms, and the young green fruit, are often seeu at the same time ; while several ol the shrubs and plants, bloom nearly ali the year. Jn the centre of an open spot, generally bare of high trees, a small hut may

be seen, often termed entirely of the palm. Its trunk, split into poles, and tied lirmly together by strips of bark fiom Majaquay, (than which no rope could be stronger), forms the frames and rafters- T he footstalk, or part of the leal that encircles the trunk, is spread out, and seweil to the sides of the hut, and being about live leet long and thtee wide, and as impervious to rain as a bide, forms an excellent protection to the weather. The roof is next thatched w ith the long stems to which the leaflets are attached, cut into pieces three feel long and tied to the rafters, forming a covering about a foot thick, through which neither heal nor wet can penetrate. The door and window shutter alone are of plank, ihe floor being of clay or mud, according to the soil on which it is built. The furniture within accord well with the simple structure ; a col, a bench, a table, and a shelf, with perhaps a chest, comprising the whole; while two or three plates, and an unglazed clay cooler, commonly termed a water monkey, and a tew cups lor coffee, formed his breakfast and his dinner sets. Nothing can he more simple or primitive than the whole, telling plainly the few wants of the owner and his hardy habits. Adjoining his dwelling his horse is tethered under a tree, and perhaps a small house may he built close by for his fowls, which, however, often roost on the trees or in his own hut. In the back ground is his patch of plantains, on which he depends all the year round for his daily bread, and

which, from its sell propagating power, is the very plant for an indolent farmer. People this spot with a half dozen naked children, whose skin seems to have been long unacquainted with w'ater; a slovenly dressed woman, and a man in pantaloons and shirt, with a sword lashed to lus side, and spots to his cowskin shoes; and you ha.ve a faithful picture of the mass of Cubean peasants and their homes þÿ Simmund's Colonial Magazine.

The Merchant of Venice. þÿ In a publication which has been sent to us, called the Jewish Chronicle , we find the following curious statement in an article translated from I he German : þÿ þÿ Gregorio I.cti, biographer of Sixtus V., in his 11th book of the history of that Pope, relates several instances ot that þÿPope s strictest administration of justice. Among otliers, the following history is most minutely and fully stated. In the year 1587, as supposed about 10 years before Hits production of this piece, Paul Mario Sechi, a respected and rich Roman merchant, gained information that the Admiral Francis Drake had conquered St. Domingo, where Ire made great booty. This news he communicated to a Jewish merchant, Simono (Jeneda, to whom this event either actually seemed incredible, or who, for some reason, feigned it so þÿ in a word, be most stubbornly disputed the truth of this report, and after repeatedly protesting the contrary, said, I bet a pound of my flesh that the report is untrue And 1 lav a thousand scudi against þÿit, rejoined the Christian, who, in a most strange and haughty temper, caused a bond to be drawn up, signed by two witnesses, a Jew and a Christian, to the effect, that in case t he teport should prove untrue, then the Christian merchant, Sig. Paul Mario Sechi, is bound to pay to the Jewish merchant the sum of 1000 scudi, and, on the other hand, if the truth of this news be confirmed, the Christian merchant, Sig. Paul Mario Sechi, is justified and

empowered to cut with his own hand, witli a well sliaipened knife, a pound ot the þÿJew s fair flesh of that part of the body it might please him. The truth of Sir F. Drake's success soon transpired to he beyond doubt, and the Christian merchant demanded the fulfilment of his bond. In vain did the Jew oiler him 1000 scudi for the reparation of that which he staked. The pious Christian swore that the bond must be carried out. In the anguish of his soul tho Jew ran to the governor, by whose intercession he thought to per-

suade the Christian merchant to accept the 1000 scudi. The governor, however, reported this strange affair to the Pope, who, as might he well imagined, undertook the part of our þÿpoet s Portia, and condemned both parties to the galleys, from which they could only be ransomed by paying the fine of 2000 scudi each to the hospital of the Sixiine bridge. That Shakspeare had in mind this event, which had but recently taken place, and which is so closely connected with a national event, in which the greatest man of his country acts the hero, no one will doubt. But I am at liberty to question, that malice or hatred towards the Jews actuated our poet iu the permutation of þÿcharacters. Eng - Taper

A Fact. þÿ While in Georgia, Mr. C. took lodgings witn a Mr. 11 , owner of some 15 or 20 slaves. One of the number was a stout intelligent young man; very bright, when his opportunities were taken into consideration. This young man was frequently punistied in a cruel manner for his faults. After experiencing abuse, and suffering year after year, he chose to run the risk of enjoying liberty in the swamps and bogs of Geoigia, with all their 'loathsome reptiles, or being released from his suflering bv death, it taken, rather than suffer such inhuman barbarity as he had been accustomed to. Consequently, one night he fled making his way to the nearest swamp. As soon as it was discovered fie had fled, he was followed by Mr. H., his son, and Mr. C, my informant, who were led by a pack of hounds k-pt for the purpose. M r. H.. alter following some time, concluded to return, being fatigued, and left his son. and Mr. C.. to pursue the human chattel. The hounds soon warned the poor fellow -by their yelping that he was pursued. Expecting to receive more meicy from men than from dogs he took shelter in a tree to secure himself from the ferocity of the latter, and that he might better plead for pardon or better usage wiili ihe former. On the party coming to the tree in which he was lodged, fie was ordered down ; but not obeying so soon as young H. thought he ought to, lie cast his oak walking staff at him with such force that it brought him to the ground, when he immediately expired. A hole was Hug in the

ground, in which, treed from his sufferings, he was deposited with his rags. When the party returned, and informed the owner that they tiad killed his slave, he replied, þÿ that it was a pity, really a ,pity, to lose him, as he was worth 500 dollars, hut he posseessed too much intelligence to be a þÿslave. þÿ Bangor Gazette

In our last number we inserted a few brief remarks in favor of adopting tbe above method of illumining our commercial emporium, and as we find the proposition has ex i ted some little attention, by the numerous enquiries which have been put to us on t lie subject vve venture to present our readers with a more lucid explanation of advan tages which would result to the community from tbe establishment of a Joint Stock Company for the purpose ; and the almost moral certainty that the scheme, if carried into operation, w >uld be as remunerative as such an undertaking ought to be, consistent v<ith the public good ! At present but a portion ol our city is lighted, and the annual expense for a few oil lamps is considerable. In the first place, although it is absolutely necessary to light that portion of the city in dark nights for the protection of the valuable stores that are there situate, we think that it will not for a moment be denied, even hv the most obstinate of adherents to old plans and customs, that if the streets which contain the dwellings of our wealthy merchants, and opulent residents, were also lit at night, that it would conduce much to the comfort and convenience of their inhabitants. We are confident there are few who have ant on dark miserable nights when picking their wav up or down the hills on which the best residencies are situated thought how much better it would be if there were a lamp at each conspicuous corner to shed its refulgent

rays, and light the benighted diner-out, to his own domicile. We hale to see the twinkling of a lantern bobbing up and down in front of a party returning home just like an ignus futuus , only able to delude and make darkness more visible. þÿ We would lain see a handsome tinted pillar, with u powerful lamp on us apex throwing forth a flood of light and mingling its rays wiih the next friendly beacon The advantages appertaining to the use of portable gas are viz, first its superior cheapness over coal gas or any other illuminating material þÿ secondly the simplicity and cheapness of the machinery requisite to generate it þÿ thirdly, the case with which it may fie used in any situation, (no main or branch pipe) and breaking up of roads being requisite. Portable gas it is well known may tie manufactured from a variety of substances, and we believe that our island could furnish a raw material which would answer the purpose, and at the same time, give employment to a number ol poor people, but we defer this portion of the sub jeet till some movement has actually taken place. In England the cost of portable gas (m mufactured from oil) is about one larihing per hour, for a gas burner of 12 jets; and we see no reason why the cost in the West Indies should not be equally low. In our cursorv view of ihe matter in Saturday's nun- her, we estimated that a capital from #20 000 to #00.000 would be required, but ou re consideration, vve think the former sum would amply suffice, for vve estimate

for the gaseoineter, compressing engine. xc , about #5 000, for an appropriate building, a sufficient number of cylinders to contain the gas carts, horses, Aic., finings up say #10 000, which would leave #5 000 as a floating capital to pay for labour and oilier contingencies, till the returns were due.

From the St. Thomas Times, June 25, 1815. LOCAL NEWS. We were aroused this morning a little liefore 2 o'clock þÿ by the ringing of the bell at the Foil, anil the tiling of ail alarm gun þÿ con|ccturing the cause to be fire þÿ we immediately hurried forth and found our fears realized. I or uuat Iv it was bright moonlight, and the breeze was so gentle thai a was scarcely discernalile. The lite broke out in the store on the wharf belonging to Santa Stelli Esq. The authorities, the military, and militia repaired promptly to the scene of the conflagration, and every exer tion was made by 1 lie lire company, and tire volunteers lo arrest the progress of the devouring element. The spot being situate contiguous lo some of I he richest stores in our city, painful apprehensions weie exriied lest the fire should extend and destroy m its ravaging course an immense amount of property þÿ and it was alone owing lo the hearty and vigorous operations of those who worked the engines l hat the fire was cheeked in its fury. One store was burnt to the ground belonging lo Mr. Santa Stelli, and thai of Messrs. Costa Hermanns was much injured. A two storv house was pulled down lo arrest the further progress of the flames, and happily effectually succeeded in so doing. þÿ VVc are happy to stale the loss in goods is trifling c unpared to the damage which was dreaded would ensue at one period ol the lire þÿ Ihe greater portion of the goods being removed during Ihe lime Ihe buildings were in flames. The crowd w'as by no means so

great as generally happens lo be the case on similar distressing illuminations, but those who were present, it affords us much pleasure Instate, (ltd put their shoulders to the wheel (and their noble and Herculian elloris) rendered that of comparative indifference. Indeed, it is a saying of unquestionable antiquity that one volunteer is worth ten pressed

men; and lite adage was fully vetificd this morning. We are happy to be enabled to state that the fire engines were in excellent order and most efficiently served and dnected. One, the private property of Charles Dacosta 15-q. attracted particular notice þÿ it combines power with portability in a surprising degree þÿ and its performance nearly equalled that of the largest engine on the ground. We do not append a list þÿ or mention the names of any individuals who particularly signalised themselves þÿ for Ciieir name is legion þÿ and what would be our eulogistical mite among so many þÿ their self approbation will be, we make no doubt a more valuable and far sweeter reward. It is with profound sorrow that we deem it an incumbent duty to state that an almost universal opinion appears to exist among all classes of the community þÿ that the fire was the work of -an incendiary, and we learn on enquiry that at least one unsuccessful attempt has been made before to burn the same premts s. We do hope and trust that every individual in this community þÿ no matter how exalted or how humble fits station will endeavour to probe Ibis matter to the quick ; for arson is the most diabolical of all crimes þÿ the blood thirsty assassin mercifully puts his victim out of pain without delay, and is generally soon satiated þÿ he can foresee at least c Initiate the consequences of his villainy ; but the cow aidly fiend who sneaks stealthily in the depth of night when all nature is hushed in repose, with his smouldering brand to fire

the habitation of bis real or fancied foe þÿ cannot foresee þÿ much less calculate where the human agony and woe will stop when once he lias let loose the destructive clement: n >r age. nor sex þÿ not innocence, nor crime þÿ nor poverty nor wealth it þÿspares all ! perish before the ruthless destroyer þÿ and superhuman exertions ! frequently fail to arrest its scathing march till it pauses for want of materials to feed its futy. Alost fervently do we hope that the idea is a mistaken one þÿ and that the origin of the fire was purely accidental. Still more earnestly do we trust that the heartless demon will be discovered if it he true þÿ and that be may meet the condign punishment which the law justly awards to such malefactors.

A letter from Toulon states that the Emperor of Morocco was, at the date of the last accounts earnestly endeavouring to capture Abdel-Kader. The brother of the Emir Stdi Said, who had been sent to Fez to calm the anger of the Emperor, had been killed there, some accounts say by order of the sovereign, others that he fell a victim to tire populace. From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, May 20, 1845. Her Majesty's Proposed Visit to Ireland. The Queen, held a Court on Wednesday at Buckingham Palace for the reception of an address on the Throne front the Corporation of the City of Dublin. The Lord Chamber lain received the Lord Mayor at the entrance of the Throne lloom, and conducted his lordship and lite deputation to tier Majesty. The Lord Mayor read the following address from the Corporation of the City of Dublin : þÿ " To ibb Qitbbn's M st excellent Majesty address of ihe rigi1t iion the lord mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of dublin, " May it please your Majesty, þÿ Rumours having reached us that your Majesty lias been graciously pleased to express your Royal will to visit your Irish subjects in the approaching autumn, we seize w ith joy the Opportunity thus alloided us of again approaching your Majesty to reiterate our devoted attachment and loyalty to your Majesty's person and throne. " We assure your Majesty that the mere rumour of your intention lias lillcd every Irish liea > t with gladness, and we receive it as an evidence of the tender solicitude for the welfare of liehiud, which we know actuates your M »j»sty. . Warmly as your Majesty has been greeted in your Royal visits to oilier poitions of your dominions, we pledge ourselves that vour Irish subjects shall not be exceeded in the true and hearty welcome which, wriih united voice, they shall hail the landing of that Monarch on their shores who, by ber example in every relation of life (in the midst of a Court), has added lustre to the diadem

which she wears for the good of hei faithful people. " May we indulge the hope that your Majpstv will fulfil your gracious intention to visit Ireland, and there receive in person the homage of your loyal and devoted Irish subjects. " William I'ord, Town Cleik." His lordship then advanced, and kneeling near his Sovereign presented the nddress. þÿ The Queen relumed the following most gracious answer : þÿ 1 receive with cordial satisfaction this loyal address from the corporation of Dublin, 1 have ever been most auxious to consult the feelings, and to promote the happiness, of my Irish subject8. The wish which you express in gratifying terms that I should visit Ireland, is an acceptable proof of the warm attachment of the cil t i'-ris of Dublin to mv person and government. Whenever 1 may be enabled to receive in Ireland the promised wellovalty and affection of mv faithful subjects, come, 1 shall rely with confidence on the ' The Lord Mayor received from the Queen a copy of the answer, and kneeling had the honour to kiss hands Alderman O'Brien (Die Lord Mayor) and Town Councillor Patrick O'Brien, had also the honour to kiss hands, and the deputation then retired from 4he Royal presence.

Hardinge General Governor of British India on the other, respecting the sale of certain Danish East Indian Colonies to the East Indian Company. Tlift purchase monev amounts to 1,125.000 rix dollars. The treaty, which consists of nine articles relative to the treatment of Danish subjects, religious Missions, Commerce &c , refers only to the Danish possessions on the Continent of India þÿ viz, Trankebar and Serampore (the latter situated near Calcutta, arid hitherto known in Denmark as Fredenks-Nager) and a district in fialasore There is no mention made in the treaty of the Nioohar Islands, which have been for a long time claimed by Denmaik, but in which no Danish establishment at present exists. Alter having shown how flint flukes were converted into arrow points, simply tiv only pointing them at one end, so that they could immediately be fixed in a cane nr a fine wooden slick, and aftet having stated some other observations, which served as an explanation of the manufactory of flint implements in general, Air. Woisaae shortly discussed the much disputed question, if flint implements can he supposed to have been prepared by other stones, or, as some insist by metal, in which case there must then have been individuals who possessed those invaluable pieces of metal, and who furnished the remaining inhabitants with the necessary implements. In this respect it was pointed out that the old articles of stone do not belong to one and the same lime, as between l he beginning and close of the stone age, several, even many centuries intervene. On the one side, many of the simplest implements of stone could very well he manufactured bv other stones whilst it cannot be denied that a great number of the stone implements which are pre-eminently distinguished by skilful workmanship, bear proofs of being manufactured by metal. You may therefore generally take a middle course, by assuming that the oldest and more imperfect stone implements are cut out by other stones,

and in the other hand the latest which have been used at the closure of the stone age, and at the beginning of the bronze age. are prepared partly by stone, partly by metal. This opinion in the mean time requires further proof ; in particular we may hope to obtain the requisite elucidation from future discoveries of collections, toward which attention should most specially bo directed.

The new Slave-trade Treaty. (From the London Times ) All but the smallest items being not only fixed upon, but reduced to necessary form, the new slave trade treaty will bo signed before Friday next, when the Duke de Broglie will leave England. He is expected to reach Paris by Mouday or Tuesday ; Prince Charles his son, and secretary to the mission, left on Friday. The preamble of die new treaty seis foi ih that the Queen of England and King of France (die parties most deeply hound to the execution of this duty from their superior naval resources) deeming that the treaties of 1831 and 1833 have produced all the etiecl they were capable of, are desirous of forming another compact suited to the present emergency, in order more effectually to repress the slave trade. They have accordingly drawn up the present treaty, to endure for ten years; unless, at a period to be appointed (which will probably be towards the fifth year), their mutual efforts should have proved insufficient and unsatisfactory. It is therefore arranged that France shall keep on the Western coast of Africa a fleet consisting half of steamers and half of sailing ships the number amounting to not less than 27; and that the naval force employed by England will be of the same character, calibre and amount, exercising simultaneously due vigilance on thn flags of their respective nations. The treaty has been brought to this rapid termination bv tiie confidence placed in iho Duke de Broglie. It is satisfactory to stale lhat the representatives of foreign

poweis who signed the last treaty, not ratified by France, have shown the greatest goodwill on the present occasion, being animated tty feelings of amity to both the high contracting parties, and desimus under every circumstance to see energetic and etFeetivo measures employed lor i tie repression of the slave trade. The feeling which animates the British Government is that which it has displayed already iu the compact with America, namely its desire to prove its sincere wish to suppress an outrage to human nature apart from any views as regards the empire of the seas: a confirmation of the spirit which led to tins sacrifice of 20.000,000/. to liberate tbe slaves in the British colonies.

EGYPT. The fortification of Kosetta has been commenced by order of the þÿI acha, according to the plans and under the superintendence of Gallice Bey, the French engineer, who has been engaged in the erection of the fortifications of Alexandria. One or two additional officers of artillery have arrived from Fiance to assist in completing these works and organising an efficient garrison. A haitery, mounting 100 pieces of ordnance, has been lately raised Opposite the Marabout Channel (the principal entrance to the harbour), and it is proposed to establish a line of foris mounting guns of the heaviest calibre, along the coast, at every point where it is possible a landing could be attempted. Ivosref Bev has been sent to France, loaded with presents for the King and court, amongst which is a gold snuff box exquisitely chased, and set with diamonds, valued at 2000/, intended tote given to Marshal Souli 1 he Bev has orders to proceed to England, to try the feeling of the English government ou the transit question.

A LG UK I A. The Moniteur of Tuesday publishes dispatches from Marshal Bugeaud, dated Orleansville. the 24th May. The marshal reached that town On the 22d, and intended again to take the field on the 25th, and to proceed towards the Oued-el-Hardjine. þÿ Colonel de St Arnaud, who was operating in the same country, had gained an important advantage over the principal body of the revolters, assembled at Tedjenna In the night of the 20th, having obtained precise information respecting the position of the enemy he sent olf in that direction two battalions of infantry, and the entire Cavalry under the ordeis of Lieut. Col Bisson, who, at four o'clock in the morning, surprised the Beni Merzougs and completely routed them, destroying their douars and killing about 150 combatants ; 30 women were made prisoners. The colonel captured besides, 300 oxen and 2000 sheep. On the same day, being encamped on the Oued Sidi Ben- Abbed, he was informed at three þÿo clock p. m. that a large body of men \Vas advancing towards him. þÿ An hour afterwards he descried, on the neighbouring heights, between 1000 and 1200 foot soldiers drawn up in good order, and 200 cavalry in front. The colonel did not hesitate an instant to attack them. A charge of the cavalry sufficed to spread disorder in their ranks, ami the route became general. The enemy left on the field 200 killed, and the banner of the infantry feii into the hands of the victors.

(abripoed from tiii: economist ) A deep and mysterious sensation has prevailed for some da vs past among those interested in the growth of Colonial sugai, in consequence of the rumour of a discovery that according to existing tieaties with Spain we are under an obligation to admit the sugar of Cuba and Porto Uico at the same duty as we have now established lor that tiom Java, Manilla, and other free labour countries, namely, 23s 4d. per cwt. We aie not desirous to add to the alarm, of which we have already seen symptoms consequent upon this discovery ; and we may at ike outset sav, that we believe, as fur ns regards the interests of our West India planters, there is no occasion for any alairn whatever. We shall however he glad if the right, which, as we shall show, is unquestionable on the part of Spain to demand admission tor sugars of Cuba and Poito Rico, on the terms of the most lavoured nations, shall lead to the abolition of that distinction which owr law now makes between the produce of countries employing slave labour and treelabour þÿ a distinction w hich, while it makes no real difference under present circumstances, either in the amount of protection to the planter, or in price to the consumer ; and while it, therefore, is totally inoperative for the professed object for which it was established (the discouragement of slavery) is> yet nevertheless a serious inierrwption to our good understawdii g with some of the most important countries with which we have

commercial relations, and threatens the f s of some of those best markets and especially that of Brazil. Our treaties wiih Spain, which, in our vii w, establish the uwquesti» liable tight of that country to demand lor its colonies the privileges in question, run through the period from 1667 to 1S14, in one continum s and unbroken chain in regard to this right. The first and most extensive treaty of commerce which we find between this country and Spain was signed at .Madrid on the 13th (23rd) of May, 1667, and consists of no fetter

. fc..r ii than fifty articles. That treaty, confirmed by all others following, seven or eight in number, and during the period of nearly 00 years stipulate in the most direct terms, that the two nations shall, in their commercial transactions, mutually enjoy the same rights and pnv only the same duties as ate exacted from the most favoured nations who trade with the other. The w»rds of the treaty of Utrecht, dated November, 1713, are most explicit, and may be taken as a sample of the 1st. TREATY OF UTRECHT, Nov. 1713. þÿ I þÿ The treaty of peace, commerce, and alliance, concluded at Madrid, between the crowns of Great Britain and Spain the 13- 23d dav of May 1607, is ratified and confirmed bv this treaty, and for the greater strengthening and confirmation of the same, it has been thowght proper to insert it word for word in this place together with the royal cedulas or ordinations annexed to it. þÿ II þÿ The subjects of their majesties, trading respectively in the dominions of their said majesties shall not be hound. In pat/ great tr duties or other imposts whatsoever, for their imports or exports than shall be exacted of and paid by, the subjects of the most favoured nation ; vnd if it shall happen in lime to come, that any diminution of duties, or other advantages, shall, be, granted by either side, to any foreign nation, the subjects of each crown shall reciprocally and fully enjoy the same. And as it has heen agreed, as is above mentioned, concerning the rates of duties, so it is or-

dained as a general rule between their majesties, that all and every one of theit subjects shall, in all lands and places subject to the c immand of their respective majesties, use and enjoy at least the same priviliges, liberties, and immunities concerning all imposts or duties whatsoever, w/lich relate to pet sous, wares, merchandise, ships, freighting, mariners, navigation, and commerce, and enjoy the. same favour in all things (as well in the courts of justice as in all those things which relate to trade or any other trade whatsoever,) as the most favoured nation, uses and enjoys, nr may use and enjoy for the future, as is ex plained more at large in the 38 ill article of the treaty ef 1667, which is specially inserted in the foregoing article." The latest treaty between this country and Spain, is that of August, 1814, which confirms all the preceding by the following opening article : þÿ TREATY OF MADRID, ArnusT, 1814. þÿ þÿ It I is agreed that, pending the nego. tiatio of a new treatv of commerce, Great Britain shall tie admitted to trade with Spain upon the same condition as those which existed previously to the year 1705. All the treaties of commerce which at that period subsisted between the two nations being hereby ratified and þÿconfirmed. And thus the matter rests at this day, the last named treaty being still in force. We have examined lire whole of the treaties from 1667 to 1814. relating to commerce, anti there is hot one word throughout which in ariv way tends to abrogate the provision for

reciprocal intercourse on the most favoured terms, which more strikingly than any other principle, pervades the whole of the treaties we have quoted. The question has indeed been started, whether or not these privileges extend to the produce of the colonies of Spain or are only confined to that of iici European teiritory.

S 'J. <5 3S B a 2 A T 3t 3. We cannot, however, see any ground for such a reading of the treaties. On the contrary, their general spirit would lead us to infer that many of them were made more in reference to the produce of the colonies ol the respective countries than to that of the patent country. Moreover, the language of these treaties appears to us, in the most ample manner, to extend the privileges to the subjects of each country, in any their lands" þÿ or territories, in ail matters þÿ " concerning their persons or þÿtrade, and "as to all duties' impositions, or customs whatsoever, relating to persons, goods, and þÿmerchandizes It is then desirable that we should consider what will be the effect of the admission of the prodtiC# of the Spanish colonies at the duty 23s. 4d. The produce of (Julia was estimated last year at 155,000 tons, and, that of Porto Rico, at 35 000 tons þÿ together 190,000 tons; while, Irom the whole of the British possessions in the Bast arid the H est, we imported no mote than 201.000 tons. þÿ The produce of Cuba will, however, very little exceed hall of that quantity in the pre sent year owing to the destruction caused by the hurricane in the autumn of last year. hooking only at these relative quantities, we cannot be surprised that the Colonial planter should feel somewhat alarmed at such au apparent competition. It has always been our opinion, since the distinction between slave labour and free labour sugar was first established in the session of last year that limiting the competition to the latter would

practically give no advantage in price either to the bee labour sugar or to that of Colonial growth; and that slave-latioui sugar would he raised as much m price by the additional consumption ol this country, consequent upon the admission ol tree labour produce, as the latter would. We have always contended that, as the quantity of free labour sugar which would be available for this market would be mote than we could consume at the existing differential duly, and, therefore, as a considerable portion would have to sell in the same maiket as slave grown sugar, the price of the two must remain the same. Il the additional consumption of ibis country raised the price, by withdrawing from other markets a portion ol their present supply, all kinds of sugar would be equally affected. So far as experience has gone, our anticipations have proved perfectly accurate, although, as yet, the quantity certificated sugar of which has arrived has been comparatively small, it is quite clear that slave-labour sugar has advanced in price equally with free-labour ; and that t lie relative prices are at least as high as bel'oie. If this he so with our supply of sugar, subject lo the 23s 4d. duty, limited to the produce ol Java, Manilla. Arc., how much more so will it be if the produce of Cuba and I'm to Rico are also to be admntod at the lower duty. Mlave-iubour and freelabour foreign sugar will be. as they are at this moment, relatively the same price, both being directly or indirectly detet mined by

the price ot our Colonial sugar, and the differential rale ot duly between that and freelabour produce. So that neither the producer of Colonial sugar nor the consumer at home is im any way interested in the distinction kept up; nor can any ellect be produced by it m favour of the abolition of the slave liade. The same advance which has taken place on freelabour sugar has equally taken place on slave labour, and if a higher price is to encourage slavery, we accomplish it hi this moment ns much as if we consumed Brazil sugar. And now, when it appeais inevitable that wr. must extend to Cuba and Porto Rico, as we have already done lo Venezuela and the United

- þÿ þÿ m þÿStates t , fie privilege interior d only for lirelabour produce, we cannot conceive on wtiat ground Mimsteis can pci severe in the exclusion ol the pinduce of Biazil especially when we see with what serious consequences that policy now tinea tens us.

The following is extracted from a lengthened article in the London Mom. Chronicle, on the same subject : þÿ þÿ For several days past, since this discovery was made, much excitement has prevailed among those connected with the cultivation of sugar in our colonies. And when we consider that the two Spanish islands pioduce mote sugar than all our West India islands together, the anxiety displayed is not a matter of surprise. We have, however, so often on lonuer occasions, shown that the distinction set up between lie produce of (fee labour and slave labour was not calculated is, any way lo add in the protection of the planter, to influence the niice lo the consumer, or lo give any preference in price to sugar the produce ol Java, which was not immediately obtained also by that id Biazil in the open markets. Hint it ts uivlieeessurv to slate at any length our reasons for saving that this discovery, hone er alai tiling hi liist sight, is m no way calculated to inteilere with the existing protection atlhided to our colonies, or to cheapen sugar to (lie eonsurner. For the fact is that till the advantage which free labour sugar has obtained by heing introduced lor consumption here has heen equally communicated to slave labour sugar, either for refining to bond, or for sale in continental markets We have morel v created a certain vacuum in Holland, hv withdrawing a portion of their usual supplies from Java, which has been instantly filled up by sugar from Brazil. " But where, then is the virtue of this

policy lor the suppression ol slavery ? If n higher price tor sugar is lo encourage slavery and the slave trade, then do we as effectually promote them by our present policy as if Brazilian produce were used in every house in the country. A high price obtained Im refining in bond, or for consumption in Holland. is as acceptable to the planter it-. Brazil ss if obtained directly from the consumers of this country. Bin is this distinction still to b« kept up? If so. it) whom is it to he applied f One by one, all the slave countries are released from its restriction, until Biazil, which was at tiist thought to he i fie onlv country that could claim exemption, stands as the only one to which the law will apply, unless, indeed, Mr. Gladstone may have discovered that slaves are used in Siam. We have had of late frequent occasion to refer to the baneful consequences of the invidious policy which we thus puisne towards Brazil þÿ a policy which will now lie still more invidious when we me obliged to extend these privileges to (Juba and þÿI otlo Rico. We find the following letter, which will prove interesting to our readers, in the liuies of Saturday : þÿ Sir, þÿ The state of Vesuvius is now so interesting that a short desciptiou of it would doubtless be acceptable to your readers.-- Brovunis to the lust eruption, which took place on the 1st of January, 1839, I fie crater was completely filleu up, and from the cen're of it arose a small cone, just visible at Naples above the tint of the crater, from which issued fire and vapour. The effect of the eruption was to change entirely this slate of þÿthings the contents of the crater were blown out, leaving a vast abvss of the depth ol nearly 3 IK) feet, of the form of an inverted cone, from a hole at the bottom of which issued perpetually fumes and vapour. This immense cavity has for the last six years been gradually filling up. and latterly very rapidly, from the constant dischaige of scoriae and lava, and it is now nearly lull to the brim, while from the centre rises a cone visible fiom Naples, und about 30 feet high, which is sending forth abundant fumes, and liquid lava, winch may now be seen running down the outside of the mountain. a scene would fie imperfect. The news was brought by the tl. S. steamer Princeton , which arrived at Annapolis on Thuisday last. That the gov. eminent of Texas doth consent that the people and territory of the republic of Texas mav he erected into a new state, to lie called the state of Texas, with a republican form of government, to he adopted hv the people of

said republic, by deputies in convention assembled, in order that the same may be admitted as one ot the states of the American Union, and said consent is given on the terms, guatantees and conditions set forth in the preamble to this joint resolution. See. 2. Lie it further regained. London: þÿ In coming from Lechelies hither, we touched at Juan oe Novo, where 1 had an opportunity of seeing lor the first time an island of purely coral formation. A TRIBUTE TO TRUTH, or a SUPPLEMENT to þÿ PROSPECTS OF CHRISTIANITY IN CHINA " Bell's Weekly Messenger June 20, 1845.

We feel greet pleasure, in stating that the toleration of the Christian religion in China has been finally confirmed by the Emperor. Our readers we presume are aware that the edicts which heretofore forbid the Chinese to embrace Christianity were enacted solely by the Emperor himself; without the concurrence of any religious body at present existiig in China. These edicts were for a time revoked under the reign of the Emperor Ivan-lii, but were again brought into force about a century ago, and executed with the utmost rigour down to the present time, li is certain bevond a doubt, that it is to tbe French mission we owe the abolition of these terrible laws. Ki-Ying the representative of the Emperor, in one of his letters to the French says that a Religion which forbids ev il and commands good cannot be a false one. And he adds, that as this Religion is professed by the gtcat Emperor of the French, and by the noble Nation of which be is a Soveieign, the abolition of the laws, which forbid iis exercise in China would be the best means of continuing a friendly alliance between tbe two t «untries þÿ To England then is due the honom of opening China to Commeice, but France lias opened her to Christianity and Tolerance. So far then, the sons of Coyaia instead of throwing anv obstacle to prevent the great movement ol Christianity, as they were the first to preach the gospel in China, so now they are the first to call for the moral regeneration of that people. it could not be otherwise, for what person

even moderately acquainted with the History of literature, could suppose that the sons of l.ovala, who were foremost in pushing the Sun ot Science to his high Meridian glory, would lend a hand to shut < til ils benign rays from the minds of others þÿ þÿ tell it not in þÿGath. We smile at tbe idea of a translation of the Sei ipture being completed by Dr. Morrison in Is 19, lor in 1781 no less than hlty thousand copies ol Catechisms, Bibles Ac. translated into tbe Chinese language, weic distributed amongst them by the French Mission ; but we need not add a single word more, the anecdote of Columbus and the egg is familiar to every one.
